questions.question: A dev team audits its store against the community-maintained Top 10 list of critical web app risks — injection, broken access control, and friends. Which organization publishes it?
questions.explanation: OWASP is the nonprofit community that publishes the Top 10, ASVS, and testing guides for web application security.

questions.question: After a user's first HTTPS visit, the browser must refuse any plain-HTTP request to the domain for a year, set via one response header. Which header?
questions.explanation: Strict-Transport-Security with a max-age tells browsers to upgrade all future requests to HTTPS, defeating downgrade attacks.

questions.question: A signup flow must store passwords so a leaked database resists GPU brute force; the dev picks the adaptive Blowfish-based KDF with per-user salt. Which algorithm?
questions.explanation: bcrypt salts each password and lets you raise its work factor as hardware improves; Argon2 and scrypt are also approved choices.

questions.question: A shopping app offers 'Sign in with Google', receiving limited profile access without ever seeing the user's password. Which protocol provides delegated authorization?
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 issues scoped access tokens so third parties act on a user's behalf without handling their credentials.

questions.question: A support database swaps real card numbers for format-matching surrogates so a breach reveals nothing reversible. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Tokenization maps sensitive values to non-sensitive tokens held in a secured vault; unlike encryption, tokens are not mathematically reversible.

questions.question: A retailer hires ethical hackers in a scoped engagement to actively exploit its store and report weaknesses before criminals find them. What practice is this?
questions.explanation: Penetration testing is authorized, goal-driven exploitation of systems to validate real-world security posture.

questions.question: To stop `' OR '1'='1` login bypasses, the dev rejects any field that fails the expected email pattern, server-side. What defense is this?
questions.explanation: Input validation enforces expected format, type, and length at trust boundaries, shrinking the injection attack surface.

questions.question: A reporting service gets read-only database access even though the team's shared admin credentials would work. Which security principle mandates the minimal grant?
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants every user and process only the access it needs, containing the blast radius when accounts are abused or breached.

questions.question: Even if the server's private key leaks next year, recorded TLS sessions stay sealed because session keys used ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman. Which key exchange enabled this forward secrecy?
questions.explanation: ECDHE generates per-session keys never stored or derived from the server's key, so later compromise cannot decrypt captured traffic.

questions.question: An attacker uploads a 'photo.jpg' that browsers sniff and execute as script; the server must forbid MIME sniffing with one header. Which header?
questions.explanation: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff forces browsers to honor the declared Content-Type, blocking disguise-by-sniffing attacks.

questions.question: A script saved in a comment field executes for every visitor. Classify this XSS.
questions.explanation: Stored XSS persists payloads in server data.

questions.question: A crafted URL's script reflects back in the response and executes once. Classify this XSS.
questions.explanation: Reflected XSS returns payloads within the response.

questions.question: What XSS variant executes when page JavaScript writes untrusted data into the DOM?
questions.explanation: DOM XSS runs entirely in client-side code.

questions.question: A bank's session cookie must not hitchhike on requests forged from attacker.com; the dev sets a cookie flag to 'Strict' so browsers withhold it on cross-site requests. Which attribute?
questions.explanation: SameSite=Strict (or Lax) tells browsers not to send the cookie on cross-site requests, breaking the CSRF delivery path.

questions.question: Attackers corrupt a resolver's cached records so shoppers typing the store's real domain silently land on a phishing clone. What is this attack called?
questions.explanation: DNS cache poisoning injects forged records into resolver caches, so users of that resolver receive attacker IPs for legitimate names.

questions.question: A store adds a response header listing exactly which origins may serve scripts, neutralizing injected tag-based payloads. Which header is it?
questions.explanation: CSP whitelists permitted script/style sources, blocking injected third-party payloads.

questions.question: A form embeds a hidden random token verified on submission so forged cross-site requests are rejected. What is this anti-CSRF defense called?
questions.explanation: The synchronizer token pattern ties a per-session random token to each state-changing form.

questions.question: Attackers replay thousands of email/password pairs leaked from another breach against a login page, relying on password reuse. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: Credential stuffing automates login attempts with breached credential pairs, exploiting reused passwords.

questions.question: A user changes the URL from /orders/1042 to /orders/1043 and views a stranger's invoice. What vulnerability class is this?
questions.explanation: IDOR/BOLA exposes objects via predictable identifiers without enforcing per-user authorization.

questions.question: A bank page must never render inside another site's iframe. Which legacy header enforces that framing policy?
questions.explanation: X-Frame-Options DENY/SAMEORIGIN prevents framing; modern CSP uses frame-ancestors.
